title_original: July Jung, Kim Do-yeon and Song Sae-byeok on “Dora”
excerpt_original: A film inspired by Freud’s Dora, two decades in the making

blocks.text: July Jung, Kim Do-yeon and Song Sae-byeok on “Dora”
A film inspired by Freud’s Dora, two decades in the making

July Jung returns to Busan with “Dora”, her third feature after “A Girl at My Door” (2014) and “Next Sohee” (2022). All three have premiered at Cannes, and “Dora” arrives at the Busan International Film Festival, in the Gala Presentation section, after its world premiere in the Directors’ Fortnight in May. Inspired by Freud’s case study of Dora, the film follows an eighteen-year-old girl suffering from a mysterious illness who experiences a summer full of changes.

July Jung was joined by lead actress Kim Do-yeon, a former Weki Meki member who won Best New Actress at the Blue Dragon Film Awards for Kim Min-ha’s “Idiot Girls and School Ghost: School Anniversary”, and by Song Sae-byeok, who reunited with her for this new film, twelve years after “A Girl at My Door”.
They discussed an idea the director first had in her twenties, the long road to making it and the casting of Japanese actress Sakura Ando as Nami.
Dora is screening at Busan International Film Festival

The titles of your films are the names of their characters, from Dohee-ya (“A Girl at My Door”) to “Next Sohee” and now “Dora”, and they are all films with powerful female characters. How did Dora start?

As you say, it may well be the starting point for the films that carry their protagonists’ names. In my twenties I came across Freud’s case study of Dora and her hysteria, and I was fascinated by it. I thought that if I ever made films, I would like to make one from this story. When I first tried to write a screenplay, this was the story that came to mind. But I had never written a screenplay before, and it didn’t work.

I kept it in the back of my mind and made “A Girl at My Door” first. When that was finished, the story came back to me, and I worked hard on a screenplay. I completed a first draft and tried to get the film produced, but it didn’t happen. People who read it said they couldn’t tell what was going on, and the investors in particular said it was too difficult. I pushed for a long time and then abandoned it. After that I made “Next Sohee”, and only then did I go back to where I had started and made “Dora”.
So this may be a film you made after a long wait. What should the audience pay attention to if they want to enjoy it, or see it differently?

When this story first came to me, I was around Dora’s age. Time has passed, and by the time I was making the film I felt I had grown much closer to Nami. So two things now coexist in me: the young person I was then and the adult of an older generation I am today. If viewers wonder why I made this film, I hope they will keep that in mind as they watch.
Kim Do-yeon, you portrayed Dora wonderfully. What joy did you find in playing her, and what was most rewarding about the process?

When I first read the script, I thought Dora and I were very different. I wondered how I was supposed to understand her, because her choices were so unlike what I would have chosen, and at first she felt very far away. But as I kept talking with the director, I gradually grew closer to her. While reading the script I even sent the director a text message saying that every sentence grew more beautiful the more I read, layer by layer. So the process of understanding this story was happy and moving for me, and shooting was a joy as well.

It was an intense and difficult summer, and everyone worked hard. But it was a kind of work I had never done before. We had a Japanese actor with us, and the cinematographer and camera team came from France. All of it was new and fun, and I learned a great deal. Being able to immerse myself so deeply in a role was a precious experience for me.

Song Sae-byeok, those who saw “A Girl at My Door” will remember you, and you have come back to the director’s world, perhaps as one of its essential figures. You play Yeon-su, who becomes a catalyst for events in the film. What was it like to work with her again?

Yesterday the director sent me a few photos. They were stills from “A Girl at My Door”, a film we made twelve years ago. It’s awkward to say it myself, but we both looked rather cute. I thought, has it really been twelve years? Time passes. Now that we have worked together again after twelve years, what I felt on set, personally, was that the director is just the same as ever: the delicacy of her direction in shaping each character, and the depth of her world. She leaves things open for a long time, and then at the decisive moment she points the way. That freedom in her approach is very attractive to me, and it helped me get closer to my character.

Your young female characters often find themselves in a world of adults who dismiss their feelings and are unable to listen to them or understand them. Could you elaborate on your intention in portraying this dynamic?

Yes, Dora clearly keeps experiencing discomfort. The world Dora sets out from includes her parents and friends of her father, and the adults spend time together there, but there are also their children, including twins, and friends of her own age. It may look like a world of adults because the people with whom she exchanges emotions, forms relationships, and influences and is influenced are adults. But I don’t think her youth is what creates the root of her discomfort. She is simply the most vulnerable being in that situation.

At first the people around her are a great driving force in restoring her fragile, ill state. Then she gradually recovers and reaches the point where she can stand entirely on her own, and at that point things change abruptly. One may wonder whether they did not actually want her to recover, and I think the confusion that arises from there dominates the second half of the film. What I most wanted to explore was how Dora acts in that confusion, what choices she makes, and how she heads toward the end.
You said earlier that you first worked on a screenplay in your twenties. Is that first screenplay similar to the finished film? And what were your thoughts about the ending?

At the beginning, what interested me in Freud’s account was the relationships and psychological forces that surround the girl. But when I looked at it again after many years, wanting to make it into a film, it struck me that all of it was what that man had seen, and that was a shock. I felt almost overpowered by it. I asked myself: is Dora’s voice here? Does it really grasp what she wants? Haven’t we only ever seen her through him? From there I thought the film should overcome that account, and I wondered what would happen if I told the story entirely in Dora’s own voice. That is the big difference from Freud’s original report, and it became the driving force of the film. In his case, she never recovered, and it ended with her ill and untreated. I kept thinking about how it could become another kind of case, one in which she recovers by herself and stands up whole.

The ending was something I had already written in the first draft. But the steps leading to that ending were not sufficient, so the work kept stalling, and some parts never fell into place. In the end, the finished screenplay is not very different from the first draft. The major developments are the same, but the relationships between characters and their actions, woven in tightly, changed little by little, and that is how I was able to reach the ending as it is now.
Dora expresses very subtle emotions. Kim Do-yeon, how did you prepare for the role, and how was the rapport with the other actors?

It grew as we got to know one another, and I value that process, which the actors built together. The most important process for me, and the most difficult but necessary one, was in a way similar to what I said at the start.

I remember it was probably at my first audition. I had received only excerpts, and I found it very hard. It was a scene with the doctor, with a senior actor in the other role. I read only that part without knowing the rest of the story, and I asked the director whether Dora was lying at that moment. She told me that Dora keeps telling the truth. At that moment I thought how lonely and difficult it must be for her to be telling the truth while everyone treats it as a lie. I was auditioning for her role and even I doubted her. That first audition came back to me again and again while I was preparing. I needed to keep switching perspectives, as a third party and as Dora, until I could come to know her heart. It was a process I needed, and I worked hard at it.
How did the casting of Sakura Ando come about?

One thing did change from the first draft, and this is it: the character was originally Korean. I had never imagined making a film with a foreign actor, and I had never really thought of people from other countries. Then at some point I wondered whether I could ever fully understand the depth of Nami’s emptiness and loneliness. Even if I made the film, wrote it and played the part myself, there would be parts I did not know. That realization was a big one for me. At the same time I wondered: what if she were Japanese rather than Korean? And almost in the same moment, I thought: then it would be Sakura Ando.

That was my train of thought that day. But I only knew Sakura Ando as a member of the audience. I had no personal connection and no way to contact her, so I was just thinking about it by myself. Then I decided to try. I contacted her through her management and asked whether she would be interested in a film in Korea. She said she would like to hear more and see the script. I had the screenplay translated into Japanese and sent it about a month later.

Why Japanese, and why Sakura Ando? It may be because I am a great admirer of Japanese cinema. When I watch her performances across many films, I find it astonishing that every role is a completely different person, and yet there is also a sense that this is simply Sakura. I thought that in whatever part of Nami I did not yet know, or could not know, an actor like her might make it possible for a person called Nami to exist between me and the actor, and that we could build this character together. I kept thinking about it, and then I reached out. Fortunately, she read the script and said she wanted to meet, and we met.

At first she agonized a great deal over the Korean dialogue; she had never spoken Korean before. Nevertheless, she wanted to bring this film, the character of Nami, and Nami’s story with Dora to life, and that is how we came to work together. I was very lucky.
The film is rated for adults only and includes intimate scenes, a first for you. Kim Do-yeon, did you have any concerns before taking the role, and how did you feel after shooting them?

Honestly, I hardly felt such concerns at first. Even though it was my first time shooting an intimate scene, I accepted it naturally when I read the script, so I wasn’t troubled by it. In the process, the director and I talked in more detail about how we would shoot it, and she asked me many times whether I was comfortable and listened carefully to what I said. The more she did, the more I tried to understand the script: how the scene is written and why it is needed. I asked the director, and I came to see that this scene is very important in our film. Nami and Dora each carry their own wounds, and showing them fully to each other for the first time, and connecting through that, is essential to the film.

As an actor I had to shoot it, and as a person it could not be nothing to me, so I was curious how it would be expressed, and the director had very firm thoughts about it. Because she understands the female body, and therefore the feelings that go with it, so well, I came to trust that I didn’t need to worry, and that trust let me throw myself into the character. On set, my scene partner helped me a great deal and checked on how I was doing, and I relied on her. The staff were very considerate as well. We also had an intimacy coordinator. It was my first time working with one, and I came to feel it is truly necessary. Thanks to that, I was able to shoot with peace of mind.
July Jung closed the conference by saying she hopes the film will move those who watch it and draw a wide range of reactions and opinions.
